title: Gut Bacterial Peptides and Autoimmunity Potential: An In-Silico Study
author: Unknown
license_note: Confirmed via CrossRef DOI metadata: dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.ibccaiw

steps.title: Retrieve bacterial and human protein datasets
steps.instruction: Download the list of gut bacterial species/genus from the Human Microbiome Project (http://hmpdacc.org/) and obtain all annotated protein sequences for those taxa from UniProt (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/uniprot). For the 319 bacterial strains (out of 823 total) that lack species‑level information but have genus information, retrieve protein sequences for every species belonging to those genera.

steps.title: Perform homology search and select peptides
steps.instruction: Run pBLAST (protein BLAST) of each bacterial protein against the complete human proteome (UniProt). Record all homologous regions and keep only peptide matches that are at least 9 amino acids long. For each retained match, save peptide length, sequence, and the corresponding protein/gene IDs and names for both bacterial and human proteins.

steps.title: Predict HLA‑II binding and test significance
steps.instruction: Submit the candidate homologous peptides to ProPred software to obtain binding scores for 50 HLA class II alleles. Also generate affinity values for a set of random peptides taken from the same bacterial proteins. Compare binding scores between candidate and random peptides using a non‑parametric Mann‑Whitney test; a significant difference indicates stronger binding of the candidate peptide to a given HLA‑II allele. Retain all peptides (regardless of significance) for downstream analysis and visualise binding affinities in a heatmap.

steps.title: Determine bacterial protein subcellular location
steps.instruction: Upload the unique set of candidate bacterial proteins to the PSLpred server to predict their cellular localisation (extracellular, periplasmic, outer membrane, inner membrane, or cytoplasmic). Record the predicted location for each protein.

steps.title: Classify bacterial species by phylum and compare frequencies
steps.instruction: Assign each bacterial species encoding a candidate peptide to a phylum using the Microwiki.com taxonomy resource. Count the number of species per phylum and the number of autoimmune‑candidate peptides encoded by each phylum. Evaluate differences with Pearson correlation in the SISA statistical tool (www.quantitativeskills.com/sisa/) and report p‑values and 95 % confidence intervals.

steps.title: Annotate human proteins for disease association
steps.instruction: Take the 575 human proteins linked to candidate peptides and annotate them with disease subgroups using the Genetic Association Database (GAD). Classify the genes with the GAD module of DAVID (https://david-d.ncifcrf.gov/summary.jsp). Compute p‑values for disease enrichment and apply Bonferroni multiple‑testing correction. Build a distance matrix of diseases based on the number of gut bacterial species harbouring each peptide and visualise it in Cytoscape.

steps.title: Assess tissue specificity of human proteins
steps.instruction: Query the UniProt tissue (UP_Tissue) database for the 667 candidate human proteins to obtain tissue‑specific expression data. Calculate enrichment p‑values with DAVID and adjust them using Bonferroni correction.

steps.title: Perform GO and KEGG pathway enrichment
steps.instruction: Use DAVID to analyse the 670 candidate human proteins for Gene Ontology biological processes and the 470 proteins for KEGG pathway involvement. Record significant GO terms and pathways after Bonferroni correction of p‑values.
